newsitem.title: USA: Government switches affirmative action case views.
newsitem.headline: Government switches affirmative action case views.

text.p: The Justice Department urged the Supreme Court Thursday to deny an affirmative action appeal from a white teacher laid off in New Jersey because of the unusual circumstances in the case.

It urged the high court to reject an appeal by the board of education in Piscataway, New Jersey, arguing that employers may consider race as a factor in layoff decisions for purposes other than to remedy past discrimination.
The case gained prominence in 1994 when the department first changed its position and supported affirmative action programmes designed to increase racial diversity.

Under the Bush administration, the Justice Department had backed the discrimination lawsuit by Sharon Taxman, the white business teacher at the high school who lost her job in 1989 while black teacher Debra Williams was kept on.

In a move that stirred controversy three years ago, the department in the Clinton administration switched its support to the school board. But a U.S. appeals court rejected its filing, and it dropped out of the case.
When the school board appealed to the Supreme Court, the high court asked the department for its views.
Acting Solicitor General Walter Dellinger of the Justice Department adopted a new stance Thursday, refusing to back the school board's appeal.
He noted both teachers were equally qualified.
"In the real world, however, that kind of tie rarely, if ever, occurs ... This court should await a case that is more representative of real-life experience," Dellinger said.
He acknowledged the appeals court "incorrectly decided an issue of broad national significance" by barring affirmative action programmes except to remedy past discrimination.
But Dellinger said the unusual facts of the case make it inappropriate for Supreme Court review.
He said the school board carried out its affirmative action policy once in 18 years, and it later dropped the policy.
Dellinger said a better case would involve "an employer that has had more extensive experience with affirmative action and that has a continuing commitment to such a policy."
The case is pending before the Supreme Court, which will decide whether to hear the school board's appeal in the next few weeks.

The school laid off Taxman instead of Williams, who was hired on the same day in 1980. Williams was the only black teacher in the business education department. Taxman returned to work in 1991 when another position opened up.
